approachQuestion.prompt:
Grid divider

A board needs h full horizontal cut lines and v full vertical cut lines. Each required line has a positive base cost. To perform a line, cut every piece that it crosses; its total cost is its base cost times the number of crossed pieces. A horizontal line crosses one plus the number of vertical lines already performed, and conversely. Return the minimum total cost of performing every line, in any order.

Example 1: horizontal=[5,1], vertical=[3] → 13: perform horizontal 5 for 5, vertical 3 for 6, horizontal 1 for 2.
Example 2: horizontal=[], vertical=[4,2] → 6.

Constraints: 0 ≤ h,v; 1 ≤ n=h+v ≤ 200000; base costs are integers from 1 to 10^6. Each of the two input arrays is already sorted nonincreasingly. Geometry other than the stated crossing rule is irrelevant. Input is read-only. Return only the stated scalar result. All arithmetic and comparisons use constant-time exact 64-bit operations; all intermediate values fit.

options.text: Merge the two supplied descending cost lists. At each step choose the larger remaining head, add its base cost times the current opposite-orientation piece count, and increment its own orientation piece count. Start both piece counts at one.
options.feedback: For neighboring perpendicular cuts with costs a and b, their order differs in total cost by b-a when a goes first. Putting the larger first cannot cost more; same-orientation neighbors have no order effect. This justifies descending merge order and arbitrary ties.

options.text: Perform every horizontal cut before every vertical cut.
options.feedback: Orientation alone does not capture the cost. With horizontal=[1] and vertical=[5], horizontal-first costs 11 while vertical-first costs 7.

options.text: Always choose the smaller remaining base cost first.
options.feedback: This multiplies expensive later cuts. With horizontal=[5] and vertical=[1], small-first costs 11 while large-first costs 7.

options.text: Enumerate every legal sequence of decisions, evaluate each complete candidate, and return the best result.
options.feedback: Exhaustive search can find the right result, but revisits combinations of decisions that the safe local rule resolves directly. The number of candidates grows far beyond what the input limit permits.

Performing an expensive cut earlier avoids multiplying it by extra opposite-direction pieces created later. Merge the already descending costs; increment the piece count of the cut's own orientation after charging the opposite count.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze only the revealed frontier method, regardless of your previous choice. Use exactly the frontier method above as iterative scans with scalar indices, counters and accumulators. Do not copy the input and do not store a decision list. Let n be the number of input records or positions. Choose the tightest standard worst-case time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Input and returned scalar are excluded. All other live storage, including copying and any call stack, is counted. No hashing or expected-time operations are used.

feedback.reason: Each cut is processed once using two indices and piece counters.

messages.text: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
The scans do not restart for each item.
In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.

details: Every cut is taken from one of the two sorted heads once. With n cuts, work is O(n); piece counts and two head indices remain O(1) state. Numerical cut costs change products, not the number of iterations.
“Time O(n), auxiliary space O(n)”: The method stores no per-item history or copied input.
“Time O(n²), auxiliary space O(1)”: The scans do not restart for each item.
“Time O(1), auxiliary space O(1)”: In the worst case every input item can affect the answer.
